messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adebayo had always found a quiet dignity in order. For thirty years as a professor of post-colonial literature, his life had been one of carefully curated syllabi, meticulously organized bookshelves, and the predictable rhythm of the academic calendar. At fifty-nine, he was a man who believed in the power of the mind to impose structure on chaos. That belief shattered eight months ago, on the day of the storm that took his son, Femi. He hadn’t been there when the flash flood swept Femi’s car from the low-lying bridge, but he had arrived at the scene just minutes later, joining the crowd staring at the churning, brown water where the road should have been. The car was a dark shape, half-submerged. The air was thick with the smell of river mud and gasoline, a scent now permanently etched into his memory.

In the months that followed, Adebayo’s well-ordered world began to flood. The triggers were everywhere. A simple rainstorm would send him rushing to close the blinds in his office, the sight of water streaming down the glass feeling like a personal threat. Walking across campus, the smell of damp earth after the sprinklers had run was enough to make his heart hammer against his ribs. These sensory cues would ignite an immediate and overwhelming sense of danger. He described it as his body betraying his mind; a cold dread would seize him, his muscles tensing for an impact that never came, all before he could even process what he had seen or smelled. This physical alarm was inseparable from a wave of horror and guilt, a crushing certainty that something terrible was about to happen again and he would be just as powerless to stop it.

This constant state of perceived threat has, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to the world around him. He feels unable to relax, even in the safety of his own home. He sits in his armchair, book open on his lap, but his hearing is tuned to the gurgle of the pipes, his eyes drawn to the reflection of the sky in the window, scanning for clouds. Because he is always anticipating danger, his mind relentlessly hunts for the very things that cause his distress. The general stress of the semester—grading papers, department meetings, the pressure to publish—now acts as its own trigger, priming his system for high alert. In this state of anxious vigilance, the scent of a puddle in the faculty parking lot or the sight of a campus pond becomes magnified, confirming the danger he already feels. His hypervigilance guarantees he will find the evidence of threat he is looking for, locking him in a self-sustaining cycle of fear.

The consequences have been profound. Adebayo, once a commanding presence in the lecture hall, now finds his focus fractured. He has cancelled classes on rainy days, citing a sudden illness, unable to bear the sight of students coming in with wet coats and umbrellas. He avoids the university’s main library, with its large, ground-level windows overlooking the river that cuts through town. The constant, exhausting hum of anxiety has made the deep concentration required for his research impossible. He feels a profound shame over this, a sense that he is failing his students and his own legacy. His body’s reaction to danger, happening before he has time to think, feels like a personal failing, a loss of the intellectual control that has defined his entire identity.

He decided to seek help after an incident last week. A promising graduate student had come to his office, distraught over a family emergency and worried about her academic standing. As she began to cry, the sheer force of her negative emotion triggered his own. He felt a surge of horror so intense it left him breathless, the student’s tears blurring with his own memory of the muddy water. He abruptly cut the meeting short, mumbling an apology, and locked the door behind her, overwhelmed by a sense of imminent catastrophe. It was then he realized the flood was not just in his memory; it was happening inside him, and he was drowning. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation to find some dry land, to once again feel safe in a world that now seems saturated with peril.
